title: Jeremiah 38:1–6
context: The narrator names four officials who heard Jeremiah’s public message (38:2–3): those who stay in the city will die, while those who go out to the Chaldeans will live, and the city will fall (compare 21:9). The princes ask King Zedekiah to put Jeremiah to death for weakening the morale of soldiers and people. Zedekiah answers that the king can do nothing against them, and they lower Jeremiah by cords into a cistern-dungeon in the court of the guard, where there is no water, only mire. The scene is a violent attempt on the prophet’s life, recorded soberly. Both traditions read Jeremiah’s message as faithful to the word he had received, and they read the officials’ charge as the reaction of leaders who heard that word as treason.

verses.text: Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchijah heard the words that Jeremiah spoke to all the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator names four officials who heard Jeremiah’s words to the people. Arminian readers note that the message was public, so the officials’ response was a deliberate reaction to what they had heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the listing of names as anchoring the account in history; Pashhur son of Malchijah also appears in 21:1. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the plot without guessing at motives the text does not give.

verses.text: “The LORD says, ‘He who remains in this city will die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans will live. He will escape with his life and he will live.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says those who stay in the city will die, but those who go out to the Chaldeans will live. Arminian readers see a real offer of life to individuals, each able to choose the path set before them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God announcing the way of survival within his judgment on the city. Shared ground: both traditions read the word as mercy within judgment, and they name the close parallel in 21:9 without harmonizing the wording.

verses.text: The LORD says, ‘This city will surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will take it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the city will surely be given to the king of Babylon’s army. Arminian readers note that the certainty of the city’s fall stands alongside the personal choices offered in 38:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fixed outcome as God’s declared purpose for Jerusalem. Both traditions read the verse as the plain core of Jeremiah’s message, which the officials found intolerable and which later chapters record as fulfilled.

verses.text: Then the princes said to the king, “Please let this man be put to death, because he weakens the hands of the men of war who remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, in speaking such words to them; for this man doesn’t seek the welfare of this people, but harm.”
verses.arminianNotes: The princes ask the king to execute Jeremiah for weakening the soldiers and people, claiming he seeks harm, not welfare. Arminian readers see how a faithful word can be recast as treason by those who reject it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the charge as an inversion: the prophet who sought the people’s good is accused of seeking their harm. Shared ground: both traditions read the princes’ demand as unjust, without inventing a deeper analysis of their motives.

verses.text: Zedekiah the king said, “Behold, he is in your hand; for the king can’t do anything to oppose you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah answers that Jeremiah is in their hands, since the king cannot oppose them. Arminian readers see a ruler who yields to pressure and abdicates responsibility for an innocent man’s life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s weakness exposed, a man with authority who will not use it for justice. Both traditions read the verse as a sober portrait of failed leadership, without turning the king’s fear into a doctrinal point.

verses.text: Then they took Jeremiah and threw him into the dungeon of Malchijah the king’s son, that was in the court of the guard. They let down Jeremiah with cords. In the dungeon there was no water, but mire; and Jeremiah sank in the mire.
verses.arminianNotes: They lower Jeremiah by cords into the dungeon of Malchijah, where there is no water, only mire, and he sinks into it. Arminian readers see a deliberate attempt to let the prophet die without shedding his blood openly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the depth of the prophet’s suffering, recorded plainly. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene soberly as a violent attempt on Jeremiah’s life, and they do not dwell on it beyond what the text describes.
